quarterly_data.signal: CEO Jim Currier: Honeywell Aerospace is still committed to its 2030 Investor Day targets - 'that 6%-8% CAGR between 2026 through 2030' - and with the 2026 guide reset to 4%-5%, 'there will be a period of catch-up, and that period of catch-up will start in 2027' as supply output rises and more is allocated to the aftermarket. The transition pressures margins (supply investments, less aftermarket allocation), but from 2027 the productivity, fixed-cost and volume leverage 'more than offset' the costs, and 'Price will change for us starting in 2027 and through that 2030 period'; he is 'still very confident' in the 2030 algorithm, top line and bottom line.

CEO Jim Currier: the 2026 guide cut came from delays in supplier transitions and second sources and the yield and quality issues they brought; Honeywell Aerospace runs about 18-24 months behind its peer group after deep 2020-2022 cost cuts under the conglomerate. The roughly 70 critical or constrained suppliers (10 constrained, in complex machining, castings, forgings and bearings) would have been in the hundreds in 2022. At two complex-machining suppliers where it is a disproportionate share of their business, embedding dozens of its own skilled workers enabled second, third or weekend shifts and about a 30% increase year on year over the last 30 to 45 days; in bearings a supplier's move between facilities and a new second source are materializing, with 35% of total annual bearing demand arriving in the last 90 days; castings and forgings tooling is coming online. Suppliers need to grow 10, 15, 20% to meet demand. Core capabilities outsourced in the past have been brought back in-house over the last two years, with more to be done.
quarterly_data.figure: about 70 critical / constrained suppliers (hundreds in 2022), 10 constrained; about 30% output increase at complex machining; 35% of annual bearing demand in the last 90 days; 18-24 months behind peers

quarterly_data.signal: CEO Jim Currier: defense is 40% of Honeywell Aerospace, about 30% of it international defense and mostly sold at commercial pricing; the international book-to-bill is about 1.5, growing double digit. Q2 defense growth of about 3% combined domestic growth of about 10% year on year with international down about high singles, because limited supplier output is allocated to national security first. In the commercial aftermarket he has seen 'zero decline' in entitlement month over month despite air-transport pressure and demand is above entitlement; because no aircraft may leave an OEM's production site missing Honeywell parts, more output went to OE and less to spares in Q2.
quarterly_data.figure: defense 40% of business (about 30% international); international book-to-bill about 1.5; Q2 defense about 3% (domestic about 10%, international down about high singles)

quarterly_data.signal: CEO Jim Currier on technology: about 10%-11% of total revenue goes to new products and technologies (about 6% customer funded, just north of 4% internal), developed once and deployed across air transport, business aviation and defense; next-generation single-aisle technologies (bleedless architecture systems, electromechanical actuation, vapor cycle cooling, electric pressurization, hybrid systems) will be certified first on business-aviation and defense platforms. The sixth-gen Anthem avionics cockpit has started the qualification phase on other platforms, alongside work on a next-gen HTF7000 engine, APUs, Honeywell Assure electromechanical actuation and Honeywell Intune vapor cycle cooling. Navigation is in 'every single precision-guided missile ammunition system in the U.S. arsenal'; Honeywell Aerospace makes over 100,000 nav products per year and is developing alternate navigation against spoofing and jamming. He believes it can get back to its previous-generation content share on next-gen programs.
quarterly_data.figure: R&D about 10%-11% of revenue (about 6% customer funded, north of 4% internal); over 100,000 navigation products per year
